Hi Lisa —

Appreciate the quick review and great questions. Short version: Dedicated pools provide tenant isolation at multiple layers (physical allocation, runtime isolation, and process-level enforcement). I pulled together a concise pack and a diagram (attached) and added a couple of redacted microbench logs that show isolated runs. The pack includes:

- A plain-English overview of isolation controls (physical GPUs pinned to tenant pools, no hypervisor-level oversubscription in Dedicated mode).
- Runtime-level enforcement: each tenant's model processes run in isolated containers with enforced cgroups and explicit CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES pinning. We do not share the same GPU device file descriptors between tenants.
- KV cache handling: KV cache is kept in-process by default; for responses that use a shared in-memory cache we persist only shard metadata in a tenant-scoped Redis instance (not on GPU) — in Dedicated mode Redis is in the customer's VPC by default.
- Noisy neighbor mitigations: per-tenant SM scheduling limits, per-tenant GPU memory reservations (OOM guards), and optional soft real-time throttling. We also enforce per-cluster QoS policies that prevent a single tenant from exceeding reserved SM cycles without an explicit burst policy.

I've attached the diagram that shows the physical GPU assignment and the redacted perf run where Tenant A saturates an SM-limited kernel but Tenant B's latency remains within SLO because of scheduling + reservation.

If you want, Marissa can do a short 30-minute call next week to walk through the diagram and the logs.

Hi Lisa —

Following up with a bit more technical color (from runtime engineering):

1) Physical allocation and device isolation
- In Dedicated mode, GPUs are allocated to a tenant's pool and presented only to the tenant's nodes. There is no virtualization layer that multiplexes a single GPU device across tenants (we do not rely on MIG for multi-tenant Dedicated pools unless explicitly configured in a managed MIG offering). Device files (/dev/nvidia*) are namespace-isolated; container runtimes are configured with device whitelists.

2) GPU memory and KV cache
- We avoid cross-tenant GPU-resident KV cache by default. The inference runtime stores KV cache in-process to minimize copy overhead; that process is strictly scoped to the tenant's container. When persistent KV caching is enabled for cold starts, Redis instances are tenant-scoped and can be placed in the customer's VPC for Dedicated Private deployments.

3) Shared interconnects (NVLink / PCIe)
- Shared NVLink domains are only present when GPUs are colocated in a multi-GPU node assigned to the same tenant pool. We do not place different tenants into the same NVLink domain. For host PCIe, the primary risk is DMA/host memory saturation — we mitigate this by per-tenant DMA rate controls and IO QoS at the host kernel and by scheduling heavy IO-bound jobs during reserved maintenance windows if requested.

4) Noisy neighbor detection and remediation
- We emit telemetry (per-GPU SM utilization, per-process memory usage, kernel queue depth) to our metrics backend. For Dedicated pools, those metrics are retained at higher granularity and can be shared with customers under NDA. Example remediation: automatic throttling of new generation kernels when a tenant exceeds a configurable SM utilization threshold, and live migration of non-latency-critical jobs to spare nodes.

5) Evidence and tests available
- Redacted microbench logs (attached) showing isolated run.
- A short reproducible test we can run in a sandboxed cluster to prove no cross-tenant KV leak.

If FinTech wants, we can run the sandbox test with your security team observing; that tends to be the fastest way to confirm.

Cheers,
Marissa Cole
Principal Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
